# Boiler Pressure Loss

## Overview

A sealed heating system runs under a fixed charge of water and a small cushion of air or gas that lets the water expand as it heats. The gauge on the front of the boiler reads that charge, and on a healthy system it moves a little between cold and hot but returns to the same place when everything cools down again. What matters is the cold reading, taken first thing in the morning before the heating has run, because a hot gauge is always higher and tells you almost nothing on its own. If the cold reading creeps down week after week, water is leaving the system somewhere and air is taking its place. That is a slow leak rather than a sudden fault, and it is worth finding before the boiler locks out or the top of a radiator starts to run cold. I keep a note of the cold reading on the folder by the meter so I can see a trend rather than a single number. A drop of half a bar over a month is a leak worth chasing, while a few hundredths on a frosty morning is nothing.

## Troubleshooting

The causes run in a rough order of likelihood, and it is worth working down that order before you start pulling floorboards up. First is air left in the system after any work or bleeding, which looks exactly like a leak for a few days and then settles once the air has been driven out and the charge topped back up. Second is a weeping radiator valve gland, the little packed joint where the valve spindle passes through the body, which weeps a drop at a time and leaves a faint crust or a damp patch that dries back between drips. Third is a pinhole in a pipe or a joint that has given up quietly under a floor or behind plaster. On our system the culprit turned out to be the gland on the landing thermostatic valve, which had been weeping slowly enough that the damp only showed as a stain on the carpet edge. Shutting the valves on one radiator at a time is the simplest way to find a hidden leak, because a radiator that is isolated drops out of the circuit and if the gauge then holds steady you have found the branch that is losing water.

When you close a radiator off, note the gauge cold the next morning before you open it again, and give it at least a full day so a slow weep has a chance to show. Work round the house one radiator at a time, keeping a written note of which valves are shut, and do not leave a radiator isolated for more than a couple of days in cold weather. If the gauge falls with every radiator shut off, the leak is on the pipework rather than at a radiator, and that is the point at which a pressure test starts to make sense. A pinhole leak on a copper pipe under a floor can lose enough water in a week to show clearly on the gauge while leaving no visible mark in the room above, so the isolation test is worth the effort before you lift anything. If the gauge holds with everything open but drifts again whenever the heating runs, look at the joints that move most, which are usually at the boiler and at the pump.

## Steps

1. Bleed every radiator, starting at the lowest floor and working upwards, and take the cold gauge reading before you begin.
2. Top the system back up to 1.0 bar cold through the filling loop, watching the gauge as the water goes in.
3. Write the cold reading on the note by the meter, then read it again each morning for a week at the same time.
4. If the pressure is falling, retighten the gland nut on the radiator valve a quarter turn and check for damp beneath it.
5. Isolate radiators one at a time if the drop continues, and leave a note on each valve you close so nothing is forgotten.
6. Call an engineer for a pressure test if the gauge keeps falling with every radiator shut off.
7. Check the joints around the boiler and the pump for damp once the heating has run hot and then cooled again, since a joint that only weeps while warm is easy to miss.
8. Keep the filling loop valve shut and the loop disconnected between top ups, so that the cold reading you write down is an honest one rather than one propped up by mains water.
9. Photograph the gauge at the same time each morning if you are away from home, so the week of readings is easy to compare when you get back.

## Notes

I disconnect the filling loop from the mains whenever I am not actually filling the system, since a permanent connection can let mains water creep in and hide a loss behind a slowly rising charge. The inhibitor level should be checked whenever the system has been drained or topped up, because fresh water dilutes it and the pipework loses its protection. If the gauge keeps dropping after the gland has been tightened and the air has settled out, ask for a pressure test rather than topping up every week, because a system that needs constant water is a system that is corroding from the inside. I keep the last few readings on the same note, so a slow loss shows up as a line of numbers rather than a vague feeling that the gauge looks low.
